desc:
A job board lists n jobs. Job i has difficulty difficulty[i] and pays profit[i]. There are m workers; worker j has ability worker[j] and can do any job whose difficulty is at most that ability.

Each worker takes at most one job, but a job is not used up: any number of workers can take the same job. Return the largest total pay all workers can earn together. A worker who cannot do any job earns nothing.

difficulty = [2, 4, 6, 8, 10]
profit     = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50]
worker     = [4, 5, 6, 7]                  -> 100

difficulty = [85, 47, 57], profit = [24, 66, 99], worker = [40, 25, 25] -> 0

In the first example the workers earn 20, 20, 30 and 30.
hints: Workers do not compete: each worker independently takes the best-paying job they are able to do. What is the answer for a single worker?
For one worker with ability a, you want the maximum profit among jobs with difficulty at most a. Doing that scan for every worker is O(n * m); sorting can share the work.

Sort jobs by difficulty and keep a running maximum of profit. Sort the workers by ability and sweep both lists with one pointer into the jobs: for each worker advance the pointer over all jobs they can do, updating the running best, then add that best.
editorial: Because a job can be taken by any number of workers, the workers are independent and each one should simply take the best job within their ability. The total is the sum of those best values.

To avoid checking every job for every worker, sort the jobs by difficulty and the workers by ability. Maintain best, the maximum profit among the jobs whose difficulty is at most the current worker's ability. As abilities increase, the set of doable jobs only grows, so a single pointer moving forward through the sorted jobs is enough. Add best to the answer for each worker.
Time O(n log n + m log m), space O(n).
